transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I came in because... well, recently I started helping out with the safety trainings down at the plant. I only really agreed to do it because Brenda retired back in the fall and they were just so short-staffed. Brenda was there for thirty-five years, can you believe that? They gave her a lovely little clock for her mantel when she left. I don't really have a mantel myself, just a TV stand, but anyway—what was I saying? 

Oh, right. Since I started doing those trainings, I just can’t seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I’m up there pointing things out on the board to everyone. My mother had hands just like that, always scrubbing things with this awful pine soap that smelled like a cheap car freshener. But seeing my hands looking so awful... it just gets me going, and then I start thinking my face looks completely crooked in the company newsletter photos they take of us. I've pointed it out to a couple of the other girls on the line, and they swear they don’t see it at all, but... I don't know. It's just really been bothering me lately.
When you look at your hands or face and notice they look wrinkled or crooked, do you feel certain that this is true even when others tell you they don’t see it?

Well, I mean... I guess I'm not really sure if I'm certain. I know what I see, but then when the girls say they don't see it, it makes me wonder. Like, maybe it's just the lighting in the break room where they take those pictures. The fluorescent lights in there are just terrible, they really are. They installed them back in '98, I remember because that was the same year my sister had her first baby, little Tommy. He's all grown up now, working in real estate out in Arizona. He says the sun out there is just relentless. I always tell him to wear sunscreen, you know, because you just never know what the sun can do to your skin over time. But... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the girls at work. They say I look fine, but I just... I don't know, I still see it when I look in the mirror. I just can't say for sure if they're just being nice or if I'm really seeing things right.
Do you think it's possible that your view of your hands and face might not be completely accurate, even if you notice something that bothers you?

Well, I suppose it's possible... I mean, I'm not an expert or anything. My neighbor, Gary, he thinks he's an expert on everything. Just last week he was telling me how to prune my hydrangeas. Can you believe that? The man's grass is half dead, but he's giving me gardening advice. I've been growing those hydrangeas since my husband passed, and they always bloom beautifully. The secret is coffee grounds, really. You just sprinkle them around the base. I started doing that after I read an article in a magazine at the dentist's office. Dr. Miller, he's a good dentist, but his waiting room is always freezing. I always have to bring a sweater. But anyway... I guess I don't really know if what I'm seeing is completely accurate. It's just hard to ignore when it feels so obvious to me, you know?
Would you say that your concerns about the way your hands and face look are something that might be exaggerated or out of proportion to what others actually see?

Exaggerated? I mean... I really couldn't tell you. I'm just not sure if I'm blowing it all out of proportion or not. 

Speaking of exaggerating, though, my supervisor down at the plant, Dave, now he really knows how to exaggerate. Just last Tuesday, we were short maybe three boxes on pallet four, and he carried on like the entire factory was shutting down. He gets so red in the face when he gets worked up, it’s a wonder his blood pressure isn't through the roof. I actually brought him some of my zucchini bread once to try and sweeten his mood. I grow the zucchinis myself in the backyard. They get absolutely massive if you leave them on the vine too long—I mean, big as baseball bats! You have to grate them up real fine to bake with them, otherwise the bread gets much too soggy. I use my grandmother's old metal grater, the kind that practically takes your knuckles off if you aren't paying close attention... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Something about the plant?
Do these concerns about how your hands and face look cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life, like doing your job or being around others?

Well, it hasn't stopped me from working, or volunteering. I still help out at the church, you know. I usually organize the bake sale every spring. We had a bit of a disaster this year, though, because Mary forgot to bring the folding tables. She’s getting a bit forgetful lately, bless her heart, and her husband isn't much help either since he had his hip replaced. He used to be such an active man, always out in the yard... 

But anyway, I still go to volunteer and work. I just... I hesitate a lot more before going to social events that I used to really enjoy easily. And getting ready takes me so much longer now, especially if there's a training day at the plant. They always want to take pictures during those trainings for the company newsletter, and I've started just ducking out of the way when I see the camera. 

My niece, Sarah, she's always taking pictures too, on her phone. She wanted to take one of me and her dog last weekend. It’s a Golden Retriever, named Buster. Sweetest dog, but he sheds absolutely everywhere. I have to run the vacuum twice when they come over. I bought one of those new vacuums off the television last year, the ones that are supposed to be lightweight? Well, let me tell you, the man on the screen made it look much easier to push around than it actually is. My shoulder was aching for two days after I used it on the stairs... 

Wait, what was I saying? Did I answer your question about my job?

When you avoid being in pictures or hesitate before going to social events because of how your hands or face look, does this avoidance cause you a lot of anxiety or make it hard for you to do things you need or want to do?

Well, anxiety... I wouldn't say a *lot* of anxiety, no. It's more just... a nuisance, really. I still do the things I need to do. I mean, I have to go to the grocery store, don't I? Though I try to go early on Sunday mornings now, right when they open. The produce is fresher then anyway. 

Speaking of groceries, did you know they rearranged the aisles at the SuperValu down on Main Street? Completely moved the baking supplies. I spent twenty minutes looking for vanilla extract last week. I was making a batch of those snickerdoodles for the church potluck—the ones with the extra cinnamon? My mother used to make them every Christmas, and she'd always let me roll the dough in the sugar. She had this beautiful old ceramic mixing bowl with blue stripes on it... I think my sister took it when mom passed, which really isn't fair because she doesn't even bake. She just buys those pre-made cookies in the plastic tubs. I mean, who wants a cookie that tastes like preservatives? 

Anyway, I still get things done. I just don't like the pictures, that's all. Does that make sense?
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, touching your face or hands, or trying to fix how they look in photos, because these concerns bother you so much?

Well, I suppose I do check a bit. Before a class or one of those workshops at the senior center, I'll go into the bathroom and check the mirror a few times. I'll put some lotion on my hands, turn my face this way and that to see how the light hits it. Sometimes I'll even ask a coworker if I look all right. It makes me run a little behind, sure, but I always get there eventually. 

Speaking of the senior center, they just started offering a water aerobics class on Thursday mornings. I thought about joining, but I just don't know if I want to deal with a wet bathing suit at my age. Getting those things off when they're damp is like trying to peel a stubborn orange. My neighbor, Helen, she goes every week. She bought one of those fancy suits with the little skirt attached. She got it on sale at Macy's, can you believe it? Macy's! I haven't shopped there in years. Not since they closed the one at the old mall. That mall used to be so nice, with the big fountain in the middle... kids used to throw pennies in it. I wonder what happens to all those pennies? 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, yes, checking. I just check a few times, that's all. It's not a big deal.

Do you believe that the issues you see with your hands and face are due to a defect or flaw in your appearance that you think is very noticeable or serious, even if others don’t seem to see it that way?

Well, yes, I suppose I do think it's very noticeable. That's actually why I came in, to be honest. Since I started helping with the safety trainings at the plant, I just... I can't seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I'm up there pointing things out on the board. And then I start thinking my face looks all crooked in those company newsletter photos. I mentioned it to my supervisor, and she told me she didn't see what I was talking about, but I know what I see. 

It's just like when I tried to tell the contractor about the uneven tile in my guest bathroom. He swore up and down it was perfectly level, but I could tell the grout lines were off by at least a quarter of an inch. I had to hire a completely different company to come fix it. The new guy, Tom, he was much better. He even showed me how to seal the grout myself so it wouldn't get mildew. Mildew is such a problem in this climate, isn't it? Especially with the humidity we've been having. My hydrangeas are loving it, though. The blue ones are just bursting this year. I tried adding those coffee grounds to the soil like they say on the gardening shows, and it really seemed to deepen the color. Do you garden at all? It's very relaxing, getting your hands in the dirt... well, except then I have to scrub my hands for ten minutes to get the dirt out of all those wrinkles I was telling you about. 

But anyway, yes, I think it's very noticeable, even if other people claim they don't see it.
Can you tell me if you’ve ever thought that others notice or talk about your hands or face in a negative way when you haven’t actually heard them say anything?

Well, no, I wouldn't say I think people are whispering about me or anything like that. I don't really get the feeling they're staring or talking behind my back. They're usually too busy with their own things anyway.

Speaking of being busy, did you know they're changing the shift schedules at the plant again? It’s the third time this year! They’re trying to implement this new rotating system, and it is just wreaking havoc on everyone’s sleep schedules. My friend Carol—she works over in packaging—she said she was so tired on Tuesday she accidentally put her car keys in the refrigerator instead of the milk. Can you imagine? I told her she needs to start drinking chamomile tea before bed. I grow my own chamomile, you know. I dry the flowers in the sunroom. It smells so lovely in there right now, like apples and honey. I got the seeds from this little catalog that comes in the mail, the one with the hand-painted covers. They have the most beautiful varieties of heirloom tomatoes, too. I tried growing the purple ones last summer, but the squirrels got to them before I could. Squirrels are just relentless, aren't they? They'll chew right through the netting. 

But no, I don't think people are talking about my hands or face. I just don't like how they look, that's all.
Do these concerns about your hands and face bother you so much that you feel significant emotional distress, even if you don't feel anxious or avoid things completely?

Well, no, I wouldn't say I feel "distress." It doesn't make me cry or lose sleep or anything dramatic like that. It's really just... annoying, you know? Like a pebble in your shoe. 

Or, honestly, it's like those new barcode scanners they just forced on us at the plant. Management swore up and down these new ones were top-of-the-line, supposed to make inventory a breeze, but I swear the batteries die after just three hours on the floor. My supervisor, Greg, he had to call the IT department down four times on Tuesday alone. And those IT guys, they take their sweet time getting to us. They just sit up there in their air-conditioned office while we're down there sweating on the line. 

Which reminds me, I really need to have someone come look at my central air unit at home. It’s started making this awful rattling noise every time the compressor kicks on. It sounds exactly like a box of rocks in a washing machine. My neighbor said it might just be a loose fan blade, but I don't want to go poking around in there myself and void the warranty. I'm pretty sure the warranty is good for another two years. I keep all those appliance manuals in a big blue binder in the kitchen, right next to the microwave. I should probably check it tonight. 

Anyway... I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being upset about my hands. No, I'm not really upset or distressed. I just wish they looked a bit better, that's all.

Do you spend a lot of time thinking about these concerns, or do you find yourself doing certain things over and over—like checking your appearance or adjusting how you look—to try to feel better about them?

Well, I do check sometimes, yes. Like before I have to lead one of those safety classes, or if I'm going to a workshop down at the senior center, I'll go into the bathroom and check the mirror a few times. I put extra lotion on my hands, try turning my face this way and that to see if the lighting makes a difference, and sometimes I'll ask one of the girls on the floor if I look all right. It usually makes me run a few minutes late, but I always get there eventually. 

Speaking of being late, the traffic on Route 9 was just unbelievable this morning. They've got the whole right lane blocked off for some kind of utility work, and they don't even have a flagger out there directing people. It's just a mess of orange cones. I don't know why they can't do that kind of work at night when nobody is on the road. My son, David, he used to work for the highway department before he moved out to Arizona, and he always said the scheduling was completely backwards. Arizona is so nice, though. He sends me pictures of the sunsets, and they are just spectacular—all these bright pinks and purples. He's trying to get me to come visit for Thanksgiving this year instead of him coming here. I don't know, though. Flying around the holidays is such a headache. The airports are packed, and they always charge you an arm and a leg just to check a single suitcase. Have you flown anywhere recently? They make you take your shoes off and everything, and the floors are always so cold. 

But anyway, yes, I do check the mirror a few times and use the lotion, just to try and make things look a little better before I have to stand up in front of people.
Are your concerns about your hands and face specific to certain features, or is it more of a general sense that you're aging or not looking the way you used to?

Well, I'm not really sure. I haven't really thought about it like that. I don't know if it's a specific feature or just... getting older, I guess? They just don't look right to me. I did try buying this new firming lotion at the pharmacy on Tuesday to see if that would help. 

The girl at the checkout—she couldn't have been more than seventeen, still had those colorful rubber bands on her braces—she had the hardest time trying to scan my coupons for it. I always clip the manufacturer ones from the Sunday paper. Do you still get the physical paper delivered? I really only keep my subscription for the crossword puzzles and the coupon inserts. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he actually cancelled his subscription last month because he said the delivery boy kept throwing it directly into his prize rose bushes. Mr. Henderson is very particular about his roses. He's got these huge yellow ones, I think they're called Julia Child roses? They smell just like sweet licorice. I tried growing roses once by my front porch, but the Japanese beetles just skeletonized the leaves in a matter of days. You have to be so vigilant with those little pheromone traps, and honestly, who has the time? By the time I get off my shift at the plant, all I want to do is sit down with a cup of tea. 

Anyway, I'm sorry, what were you asking? Oh, right, about my face and hands. Yeah, I don't really know if it's aging or exactly what it is. I just know I don't like the way they look when I see them.
Do these concerns about your hands and face take up a lot of your time or make it hard for you to function normally in your daily life, like at work, at home, or when you're out with other people?

Well, no, it hasn't stopped me from working or doing my volunteer stuff. I mean, I'm still showing up. I am a bit slower getting ready for those safety trainings, like I said. And lately, I've started ducking out of photos or kind of hesitating before I go to social things I used to really enjoy. 

Like the potluck we had last Sunday at the church hall. I almost didn't go. I ended up going, but I made sure I was the one cutting the casseroles so I could stand behind the serving table. Mary Anne brought her famous green bean casserole, the one with the little crispy onions on top. She uses the canned onions, but I swear she does something to them because they never get soggy. I asked her for the recipe once, and she just tapped her nose and said it was a family secret. Can you believe that? A family secret for green bean casserole. Her grandmother probably got it off the back of a Campbell's soup can in 1960. 

Speaking of soup, I've been trying to eat more of it lately. Less heavy meals, you know? I bought this big stock pot at a yard sale a few weeks ago. Only paid four dollars for it, and it's heavy-bottomed stainless steel. The lady selling it said she was downsizing to a condo because she didn't want to deal with mowing her lawn anymore. I can understand that. My push mower is so heavy, and it takes me almost two hours to do the front and back. I really should hire the teenager down the street, but he charges twenty dollars, and he always misses the patch right by the mailbox. 

But anyway... what did you ask? Oh, right, about it making it hard to function. No, I still do everything I need to do. I just hesitate a bit more with social stuff and photos, and take a little longer getting ready, but I get it done.

Do these concerns about your hands and face take up so much of your time or attention that it feels hard to focus on other things, or has it ever made you seriously consider avoiding your responsibilities or relationships with others?

Well, no, it's not like that. I'm not avoiding my responsibilities or anything. I still go to work, I still see my friends. It doesn't take up all my attention. I mean, I notice it, but I'm not sitting around all day just staring at my hands. 

Though speaking of hands, I really need to get my gardening gloves replaced. The thumb on the right one has a huge hole in it, and I got the nastiest blister last weekend when I was pulling weeds by the back fence. Those dandelions are just relentless this year. I swear, you pull one up by the root, and three more pop up the next day. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson—the one with the roses—he uses this awful chemical spray on his lawn, and I just know it's going to drift over and ruin my tomato plants. I've got two Big Boy tomatoes and a cherry tomato plant in these nice ceramic pots on the patio. I found the pots at a discount store last spring. They were half off because one of them had a tiny chip on the rim, but you just turn that side toward the wall and nobody even notices. I'm hoping to make my own salsa this year if the cherry tomatoes do well. I found this recipe online that uses roasted garlic and fresh cilantro. Some people say cilantro tastes like soap to them, which I think is just fascinating. It's a genetic thing, did you know that? My sister can't stand it, but I think it's lovely. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I'm not avoiding my life or anything like that. I still do what I need to do.
Would you say that the way your hands and face look bothers you more than it seems to bother other people who see you?

Well, yes, I suppose it does bother me more than other people. I mean, that's exactly why I came in to see you. Ever since I started helping out with those new safety trainings at the plant, I just... I can't seem to stop noticing how wrinkly and uneven my hands look whenever I'm pointing things out on the diagrams. And then it got me looking at my face, especially in the company newsletter photos. I keep thinking my face looks crooked, but when I mention it to my coworkers, they look at me like I'm crazy and say they don't see it at all. 

Speaking of the newsletter, they actually switched to a glossy paper last month. It's much thicker, almost like a magazine, but the ink smells awful. It smells like... I don't know, burning tires and cheap perfume? I told Brenda in HR about it—she's the one who puts the newsletter together—and she said they got a deal on a new local printer. Brenda is always looking for a bargain. She's the one who told me about this outlet mall three towns over where you can get name-brand shoes for next to nothing. I went there once, but it was just a madhouse. People pushing and shoving over discounted sneakers. I ended up buying a soft pretzel and leaving. The pretzel was very good, though. It had that coarse salt on it, and I got a little cup of cheese dip. I always feel a little guilty eating cheese dip, but sometimes you just have to treat yourself, you know? My doctor—my regular doctor, Dr. Evans—told me my cholesterol was creeping up a bit at my last physical, so I've been trying to watch the cheese. He told me to eat more oatmeal. 

But anyway... yes, I think it definitely bothers me more than anyone else. They say they don't see what I'm seeing, but I just can't stop noticing it when I'm up there doing the trainings.
Do you feel that the issues you notice with your hands or face are something that most people would probably not even see unless you pointed them out?

Well, yeah, exactly like I was just saying a minute ago. I mean, they tell me they don't see it at all. But ever since I started doing those safety trainings, I just can't stop staring at how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I'm pointing at the charts. We use those little laser pointers now, you know? The ones that make a little red dot on the wall. 

My cat, Barnaby, goes absolutely crazy for those things. I bought him this little toy mouse that shines a laser out of its nose, but the batteries died in two days. They take those tiny little button batteries that cost an arm and a leg. I went down to the pharmacy to get some, and the girl at the register—she couldn't have been more than seventeen—had to call a manager over just to unlock the plastic case they keep them in. It took fifteen minutes just to buy batteries! And then I get home, put them in, and Barnaby doesn't even care anymore. He'd rather bat around the little plastic pull-ring from the milk jug. Cats are funny that way, aren't they? You buy them fancy things and they just want to play with the garbage. 

Anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I start thinking my face looks all crooked in those newsletter photos, and I'll point it out to the girls at work, and they just look at me like I'm crazy and swear they don't see it. So I guess most people really don't notice it until I say something, and even then they don't seem to get it.
Do you feel that the way your hands or face look makes you unattractive or deformed in a way that changes how people see you or how you feel about yourself?

Well, no, I wouldn't use words like deformed. That's a bit extreme, isn't it? I mean, I don't think I look like a monster or anything. I just think my hands look terribly old and wrinkly, and my face looks a bit lopsided in those pictures. But no, I don't think it changes how people see me. They still treat me exactly the same at the plant. 

Speaking of the plant, they just put in a new vending machine in the breakroom. It's one of those fancy ones with the glass front where you can watch the little robotic arm go grab your snack and drop it in the bin. It's supposed to stop things from getting stuck, but just yesterday, Frank from shipping bought a bag of those jalapeño potato chips, and the arm just stopped halfway down. Just froze right there with the chips dangling. Frank was so mad, he started shaking the machine, and the safety manager had to come over and tell him to stop. They put an "Out of Order" sign on it, which is a shame because I was really looking forward to getting a pack of those little peanut butter crackers. I love those things with a cup of coffee around three o'clock. It just gives you that little boost to get through the rest of the shift, you know? I usually bring my own coffee in a thermos, though, because the coffee they make in the breakroom is just awful. It tastes like they've been using the same grounds since 1998. 

But anyway, no, I don't feel deformed or anything like that. I just don't like how wrinkly my hands are, but I guess it doesn't really change how people treat me.

Would you say that the time you spend thinking about or checking your hands and face has become so frequent or intense that it feels like it’s taking up too much of your day, even if it doesn’t stop you from doing other things completely?

Well, it hasn't stopped me from working or volunteering, if that's what you mean. I still go down to the animal shelter every Saturday morning. They just got in this adorable litter of beagle mixes, and one of them has one blue eye and one brown eye. I think they call it heterochromia? My neighbor's niece has that. She's a lovely girl, just graduated from dental hygiene school. I actually went to her graduation party a few weeks ago. 

Though, to be honest... I almost didn't go. I used to really enjoy those kinds of social events, but lately I just find myself hesitating. I was just standing in front of my bathroom mirror for the longest time, just staring at my face, and it made me so late. And then when they brought the camera out for group pictures at the party, I completely ducked out. I hid in the kitchen and pretended I was getting more potato salad just so I wouldn't be in the photos. 

It was a very good potato salad, by the way. They left the red skins on the potatoes. I usually peel mine because I think the skins get a little tough if you boil them too long, you really have to watch them on the stove. My mother used to make the best potato salad with just a little dash of paprika and some celery seed. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the time. It does take up time. Like, I'm definitely a lot slower getting ready for those safety trainings at the plant now, because I'm just fussing over my hands in the morning and trying to figure out how to hold things so the wrinkles don't show as much. So it doesn't stop me completely, but I guess it does slow me down and make me avoid things I used to like.
Would you say that the way your hands or face look appears abnormal or defective to you in a way that most people wouldn't even notice unless you pointed it out?

Defective? Well, I don't know if I'd use a word like that. Like I said before, they just look terribly wrinkly and uneven to me, even if the girls at work don't seem to catch it until I make a fuss. But defective... that sounds like a broken part on the assembly line. 

Actually, we just had a whole batch of defective rubber seals come through my station last Tuesday. Thousands of them, just completely the wrong size for the valves. The floor supervisor, Tom, he was about ready to pull his hair out. He was on the phone with the supplier for two hours pacing up and down the aisle. Poor Tom, he's been at the plant for thirty years and he's retiring next month, so he really didn't need the stress. We're throwing him a big potluck in the breakroom for his last day. I'm bringing my macaroni salad. I always use those little shell pastas instead of the regular elbows, because I think they just hold the mayonnaise so much better. And you have to use real mayonnaise, none of that sweet sandwich spread stuff. My sister tried to use that sweet dressing in her potato salad for Thanksgiving a few years back and I swear, nobody touched it. It just sat there all night. 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, abnormal. No, I wouldn't say abnormal or defective. I'm not a broken valve, you know? I just really don't like how uneven and old my hands and face look, even if other people don't really notice it at first.
Would you say that the way your hands or face look appears abnormal or defective to you in a way that most people wouldn’t even notice unless you pointed it out?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? About being defective? Like I was just saying a second ago, no, I really wouldn't use a word like that. It's just the wrinkles and the unevenness that bother me, even if the girls at work don't notice until I bring it up. But I'm not defective. 

You repeating yourself like that actually reminds me of the PA system at the plant. It's been glitching all week. Every time the receptionist, Mary, tries to make an announcement, it echoes and repeats her three times. It sounds like we're in a canyon! Mary gets so flustered about it. She's a sweet lady, though. She always keeps a little bowl of those strawberry candies on her desk—the ones with the wrappers that look like actual strawberries? I don't know where she finds them, I never see them at the regular grocery store. 

I usually do my shopping at the local market on Elm Street because they have the best produce section. The tomatoes at the big chain stores are always so mealy and pale, you know? You can't make a decent sandwich with a mealy tomato. You need a good, firm beefsteak tomato, maybe a little salt and pepper, some crisp lettuce, and a nice sourdough bread. My grandmother used to bake sourdough from scratch. She had this starter that she kept alive for something like fifteen years in a little crock on her counter. 

But anyway, yeah, I think we're going in circles here, doctor! Like I said, I just don't like how old my hands look, but I wouldn't call myself abnormal.

My doctor—my regular doctor, Dr. Evans—told me my cholesterol was creeping up a bit at my last physical, so I've been trying to watch the cheese. He told me to eat more oatmeal. 

But anyway... yes, I think it definitely bothers me more than anyone else. They say they don't see what I'm seeing, but I just can't stop noticing it when I'm up there doing the trainings.

Well, yeah, exactly like I was just saying a minute ago. I mean, they tell me they don't see it at all. But ever since I started doing those safety trainings, I just can't stop staring at how wrinkly and uneven my hands look when I'm pointing at the charts. We use those little laser pointers now, you know? The ones that make a little red dot on the wall. 

My cat, Barnaby, goes absolutely crazy for those things. I bought him this little toy mouse that shines a laser out of its nose, but the batteries died in two days. They take those tiny little button batteries that cost an arm and a leg. I went down to the pharmacy to get some, and the girl at the register—she couldn't have been more than seventeen—had to call a manager over just to unlock the plastic case they keep them in. It took fifteen minutes just to buy batteries! And then I get home, put them in, and Barnaby doesn't even care anymore. He'd rather bat around the little plastic pull-ring from the milk jug. Cats are funny that way, aren't they? You buy them fancy things and they just want to play with the garbage. 

Anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I start thinking my face looks all crooked in those newsletter photos, and I'll point it out to the girls at work, and they just look at me like I'm crazy and swear they don't see it. So I guess most people really don't notice it until I say something, and even then they don't seem to get it.

patient.answer:
Well, no, I wouldn't use words like deformed. That's a bit extreme, isn't it? I mean, I don't think I look like a monster or anything. I just think my hands look terribly old and wrinkly, and my face looks a bit lopsided in those pictures. But no, I don't think it changes how people see me. They still treat me exactly the same at the plant. 

Speaking of the plant, they just put in a new vending machine in the breakroom. It's one of those fancy ones with the glass front where you can watch the little robotic arm go grab your snack and drop it in the bin. It's supposed to stop things from getting stuck, but just yesterday, Frank from shipping bought a bag of those jalapeño potato chips, and the arm just stopped halfway down. Just froze right there with the chips dangling. Frank was so mad, he started shaking the machine, and the safety manager had to come over and tell him to stop. They put an "Out of Order" sign on it, which is a shame because I was really looking forward to getting a pack of those little peanut butter crackers. I love those things with a cup of coffee around three o'clock. It just gives you that little boost to get through the rest of the shift, you know? I usually bring my own coffee in a thermos, though, because the coffee they make in the breakroom is just awful. It tastes like they've been using the same grounds since 1998. 

But anyway, no, I don't feel deformed or anything like that. I just don't like how wrinkly my hands are, but I guess it doesn't really change how people treat me.

patient.answer:
Well, it hasn't stopped me from working or volunteering, if that's what you mean. I still go down to the animal shelter every Saturday morning. They just got in this adorable litter of beagle mixes, and one of them has one blue eye and one brown eye. I think they call it heterochromia? My neighbor's niece has that. She's a lovely girl, just graduated from dental hygiene school. I actually went to her graduation party a few weeks ago. 

Though, to be honest... I almost didn't go. I used to really enjoy those kinds of social events, but lately I just find myself hesitating. I was just standing in front of my bathroom mirror for the longest time, just staring at my face, and it made me so late. And then when they brought the camera out for group pictures at the party, I completely ducked out. I hid in the kitchen and pretended I was getting more potato salad just so I wouldn't be in the photos. 

It was a very good potato salad, by the way. They left the red skins on the potatoes. I usually peel mine because I think the skins get a little tough if you boil them too long, you really have to watch them on the stove. My mother used to make the best potato salad with just a little dash of paprika and some celery seed. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the time. It does take up time. Like, I'm definitely a lot slower getting ready for those safety trainings at the plant now, because I'm just fussing over my hands in the morning and trying to figure out how to hold things so the wrinkles don't show as much. So it doesn't stop me completely, but I guess it does slow me down and make me avoid things I used to like.

patient.answer:
Defective? Well, I don't know if I'd use a word like that. Like I said before, they just look terribly wrinkly and uneven to me, even if the girls at work don't seem to catch it until I make a fuss. But defective... that sounds like a broken part on the assembly line. 

Actually, we just had a whole batch of defective rubber seals come through my station last Tuesday. Thousands of them, just completely the wrong size for the valves. The floor supervisor, Tom, he was about ready to pull his hair out. He was on the phone with the supplier for two hours pacing up and down the aisle. Poor Tom, he's been at the plant for thirty years and he's retiring next month, so he really didn't need the stress. We're throwing him a big potluck in the breakroom for his last day. I'm bringing my macaroni salad. I always use those little shell pastas instead of the regular elbows, because I think they just hold the mayonnaise so much better. And you have to use real mayonnaise, none of that sweet sandwich spread stuff. My sister tried to use that sweet dressing in her potato salad for Thanksgiving a few years back and I swear, nobody touched it. It just sat there all night. 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, abnormal. No, I wouldn't say abnormal or defective. I'm not a broken valve, you know? I just really don't like how uneven and old my hands and face look, even if other people don't really notice it at first.

patient.answer:
Wait, didn't you just ask me that? About being defective? Like I was just saying a second ago, no, I really wouldn't use a word like that. It's just the wrinkles and the unevenness that bother me, even if the girls at work don't notice until I bring it up. But I'm not defective. 

You repeating yourself like that actually reminds me of the PA system at the plant. It's been glitching all week. Every time the receptionist, Mary, tries to make an announcement, it echoes and repeats her three times. It sounds like we're in a canyon! Mary gets so flustered about it. She's a sweet lady, though. She always keeps a little bowl of those strawberry candies on her desk—the ones with the wrappers that look like actual strawberries? I don't know where she finds them, I never see them at the regular grocery store. 

I usually do my shopping at the local market on Elm Street because they have the best produce section. The tomatoes at the big chain stores are always so mealy and pale, you know? You can't make a decent sandwich with a mealy tomato. You need a good, firm beefsteak tomato, maybe a little salt and pepper, some crisp lettuce, and a nice sourdough bread. My grandmother used to bake sourdough from scratch. She had this starter that she kept alive for something like fifteen years in a little crock on her counter. 

But anyway, yeah, I think we're going in circles here, doctor! Like I said, I just don't like how old my hands look, but I wouldn't call myself abnormal.

opening_question.intent: Establish the patient's reason for seeking psychiatric evaluation
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with persistent, preoccupying concerns about perceived defects in her hands and face that are not noticeable to others, leading to repetitive checking behaviors and mild functional impairment in social contexts. These symptoms align most closely with Delusional Disorder, Somatic Type (F22), as the beliefs are non-bizarre, focused on a realistic concern (aging appearance), and held with unshakable conviction despite lack of objective evidence. Schizophreniform disorder (F23.2) and unspecified schizophrenia spectrum disorder (F23.9) were considered but ruled out due to absence of prominent psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, disorganized thinking, or negative symptoms.
